prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The White House is blasting Congressional Democrats for not sending a bill that would fund veterans' care programs to the president's desk by Veterans Day. The White House's Dana Perino accused Democrats of holding veterans care funding hostage. "There's absolutely no reason that the veterans' bill could not have been signed by the president today, except for the political games that the Democrats decided to play with it," White House press secretary Dana Perino said Sunday in Crawford, Texas. Congressional Democrats had attached legislation funding veterans programs to a $150.7 billion bill that also funded a number of domestic priorities, including health, labor and education. Democrats also added $3.7 billion to what the president budgeted for veterans programs. The labor-health-education bill would increase funding by more than $10 billion over last year's funding for those programs. The president has threatened to veto the bill because of the added spending. The House passed a health-labor-education bill 269-142 last week with the veterans funding attached, but the Senate later voted to strip out the veterans funding and send the health-labor-education bill to the president. Perino accused the Democrats of "trying to hold hostage our veterans to extra domestic spending or increases in taxes." "The president wants clean legislation, a clean bill to fund the veterans," Perino said. On Saturday, the Democratic congressional leadership sent a letter to President Bush saying they welcomed a dialogue on spending, sayings disagreements over funding levels "have never been so great that we cannot reach agreement on a spending plan that meets the needs of the American people." "Key to this dialogue, however, is some willingness on your part to actually find common ground," House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-California, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, said in the letter. The leadership said last year's Congress, which was still under Republican control, had never passed a separate bill funding veterans programs. Congress also sent to the president legislation that would fund veterans care at the levels requested by the president through December 14, the leadership said. The current funding level "is still below the $3.9 billion extra that we passed," said Nadeam Elshami, spokesman Pelosi. "We are committed to getting the extra funding that the Congress already voted on the president's desk for his signature." The leadership blamed Republican members of Congress for stalling the funding for the veterans programs by blocking its inclusion in the larger spending bill. Perino, though, said the Democrats could still send a separate bill to the president funding the veterans program that passed both chambers of Congress. "The Democrats decided not to send the president this bill," Perino said. "That has to be laid at their feet." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The White House is criticizing congressional Democrats for failing to send President Bush a bill funding veterans’ care programs by Veterans Day.

White House press secretary Dana Perino accused Democrats of holding veterans’ care funding hostage.

“There’s absolutely no reason that the veterans’ bill could not have been signed by the president today, except for the political games that the Democrats decided to play with it,” Perino said Sunday in Crawford, Texas.

Congressional Democrats had attached legislation funding veterans’ programs to a $150.7 billion bill that also financed several domestic priorities, including health, labor and education. Democrats added $3.7 billion to the president’s proposed budget for veterans’ programs.

The labor-health-education bill would increase funding for those programs by more than $10 billion over last year’s levels. The president has threatened to veto the bill because of the additional spending.

Last week, the House passed the health-labor-education bill, with veterans’ funding attached, by a vote of 269-142. The Senate later voted to remove the veterans’ funding and send the health-labor-education bill to the president.

Perino accused Democrats of “trying to hold hostage our veterans to extra domestic spending or increases in taxes.”

“The president wants clean legislation, a clean bill to fund the veterans,” Perino said.

On Saturday, Democratic congressional leaders sent a letter to President Bush welcoming a dialogue on spending and saying that disagreements over funding levels “have never been so great that we cannot reach agreement on a spending plan that meets the needs of the American people.”

“Key to this dialogue, however, is some willingness on your part to actually find common ground,” House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-California, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, wrote in the letter.

The Democratic leaders said that the previous year’s Congress, which remained under Republican control, had never passed a separate bill funding veterans’ programs.

They also said Congress had sent the president legislation that would fund veterans’ care at the levels he requested through December 14.

The current funding level “is still below the $3.9 billion extra that we passed,” said Nadeam Elshami, a spokesman for Pelosi. “We are committed to getting the extra funding that the Congress already voted on the president’s desk for his signature.”

Democratic leaders blamed Republican members of Congress for delaying funding for veterans’ programs by blocking its inclusion in the larger spending bill.

Perino, however, said Democrats could still send the president a separate veterans’ funding bill that had passed both chambers of Congress.

“The Democrats decided not to send the president this bill,” Perino said. “That has to be laid at their feet.”

E-mail to a friend.

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The White House criticized congressional Democrats for failing to deliver legislation financing veterans’ healthcare programs to President Bush by Veterans Day, accusing them of using that funding as leverage.

Speaking Sunday in Crawford, Texas, White House press secretary Dana Perino said the veterans measure could have been signed that day if Democrats had not engaged in what she called political maneuvering.

Democratic lawmakers had combined veterans-program funding with a $150.7 billion package covering several domestic priorities, among them labor, health and education. They also approved $3.7 billion more for veterans than the president had requested. Overall, the labor-health-education measure would provide an increase of more than $10 billion compared with the previous year’s spending on those programs.

Bush threatened to veto the legislation because of the additional expenditures.

The House passed the combined health, labor and education measure, including the veterans provisions, by a 269-142 vote the previous week. The Senate subsequently removed the veterans funding and voted to send the remaining health-labor-education legislation to the president.

Perino charged that Democrats were attempting to make veterans’ funding contingent on greater domestic spending or tax increases. She said Bush wanted a separate, “clean” measure devoted solely to financing veterans’ programs.

A day earlier, Democratic congressional leaders wrote to Bush expressing their willingness to discuss spending. Although disagreements over funding amounts were substantial, they said, such differences had never prevented the two sides from reaching a plan addressing the needs of Americans.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid of Nevada added that meaningful talks would require the president to show some readiness to seek common ground.

The Democratic leaders noted that the previous Congress, then controlled by Republicans, had not approved an independent veterans-funding bill. They also said Congress had sent Bush legislation maintaining veterans’ healthcare spending at his requested levels through December 14.

Nadeam Elshami, a spokesman for Pelosi, said that temporary funding remained below the additional $3.9 billion approved by Congress. He said Democrats intended to place the already-passed increase before the president for his signature.

Democratic leaders blamed Republican lawmakers for delaying veterans-program financing by preventing it from being included in the broader spending package.

Perino countered that Democrats could still forward a stand-alone veterans measure that had cleared both the House and Senate. She said responsibility rested with Democrats because they had chosen not to send that legislation to the president.

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to the report. The original article also included an option to e-mail it to a friend.

The White House criticized congressional Democrats for failing to send President George W. Bush a veterans’ care funding bill by Veterans Day. Democrats had included the veterans’ funding—providing $3.7 billion more than the president requested—in a broader $150.7 billion spending package covering health, labor, education, and other domestic priorities.

President Bush threatened to veto the combined bill because it would increase domestic spending by more than $10 billion over the previous year. Although the House approved the legislation with the veterans’ provisions attached, the Senate later removed that funding before sending the remaining domestic spending bill to the president.

Democratic leaders responded by calling for negotiations. They urged Bush to work with Congress and seek common ground on overall federal spending levels so that lawmakers could resolve the dispute and secure funding for veterans and other domestic programs.

The White House accused congressional Democrats of holding up money for veterans by linking it to a $150.7 billion domestic-spending package that President George W. Bush opposed. Administration officials argued that funding for veterans’ hospitals, health care, and other programs should have been sent to the president in a separate bill rather than attached to legislation covering a broad range of domestic priorities.

Democrats rejected that criticism, saying they had tried to negotiate with Republicans and the administration over overall spending levels. They also emphasized that their proposal provided an additional $3.7 billion for veterans’ programs, presenting the increase as necessary to meet the growing health-care and support needs of service members returning from war.

The dispute reflected a broader confrontation over the federal budget. Bush had threatened to veto the combined measure because it exceeded the spending levels he had requested, while Democrats argued that the additional domestic funding was justified and that the administration was unwilling to compromise.

The Senate ultimately removed the veterans provisions from the larger package in an effort to address the veto threat and break the legislative impasse. The move, however, meant that veterans’ funding remained unfinished by Veterans Day. Both parties blamed the other for the delay, turning a measure that enjoyed broad support into another symbol of the partisan standoff over spending.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the White House accusing congressional Democrats of holding veterans’ care funding hostage by attaching it to a larger domestic spending bill.
counterfactuals.output:
**White House accuses Democrats of tying veterans’ funding to broader spending fight**

**Washington —** The White House is accusing congressional Democrats of holding funding for veterans’ health care hostage by linking it to a larger domestic spending package, escalating tensions as lawmakers face pressure to keep the government funded.

Administration officials argue that money for the Department of Veterans Affairs should advance on its own rather than be used as leverage in negotiations over other federal programs. The White House says any delay could create uncertainty for veterans who depend on VA hospitals, disability benefits and other services.

Democrats reject the accusation, saying Congress routinely combines appropriations measures and that the broader package is intended to protect an array of domestic priorities. They contend that veterans’ funding is not being threatened and accuse the administration of using veterans as a political talking point in the spending dispute.

The clash comes as congressional leaders negotiate spending levels and policy provisions across multiple agencies. Both parties say they support veterans, but they remain divided over whether the VA measure should move separately or as part of a larger legislative package.

Without an agreement, lawmakers could face another deadline-driven standoff, raising the prospect of delayed funding or a partial government shutdown. Essential veterans’ medical services would generally continue during a lapse, though some administrative functions and benefit-related operations could be disrupted.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an article on the dispute between President George W. Bush and Democratic leaders over veterans funding, including comments from Dana Perino, Nancy Pelosi, and Harry Reid.
counterfactuals.output:
## Bush, Democratic Leaders Clash Over Veterans Funding

**WASHINGTON —** President George W. Bush and Democratic congressional leaders traded accusations over funding for veterans as a broader dispute over federal spending delayed passage of the annual military-construction and veterans-affairs budget.

The Bush administration argued that Democrats had unnecessarily tied popular increases for veterans’ health care and other services to larger spending measures that exceeded the president’s budget targets. White House press secretary Dana Perino said Democratic leaders were effectively holding veterans’ funding hostage to secure additional domestic spending.

Perino maintained that the president supported providing veterans with the care and benefits they had earned, but wanted Congress to send him a clean, fiscally responsible bill rather than combine the money with unrelated appropriations.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi rejected that characterization. She said the Democratic-controlled Congress had approved a substantial increase for the Department of Veterans Affairs to address medical care, mental-health treatment and the needs of veterans returning from Iraq and Afghanistan. Pelosi argued that Bush’s veto threats and demands for spending reductions—not congressional inaction—had put the funding at risk.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid also accused the administration of distorting the dispute. He said lawmakers from both parties had supported stronger veterans programs and contended that the president was using veterans as leverage in his campaign to reduce domestic appropriations.

The disagreement reflected a wider confrontation between Bush and Congress in 2007 over the federal budget. The president threatened to veto spending bills that went beyond his proposed levels, while Democrats said the additional money was needed after years of underfunding in areas including veterans’ health, education and medical research.

Veterans groups urged both sides to resolve the impasse quickly. They warned that delays could complicate planning and hiring within the VA at a time when the department faced growing demand from aging veterans and service members returning from the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Although both parties publicly endorsed increased support for veterans, they remained divided over how the money should move through Congress and what other spending should accompany it. The result was a political struggle in which each side claimed to be protecting veterans while accusing the other of allowing broader budget politics to interfere with their care.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the November 2007 budget standoff in which the White House demanded a clean veterans funding bill and threatened to veto a $150.7 billion labor, health, and education package.
counterfactuals.output:
In November 2007, congressional Democrats combined a broadly popular military-construction and veterans appropriations measure with a $150.7 billion Labor–Health and Human Services–Education bill. The move was intended to protect increased spending for education, medical research, job training, and other domestic programs by tying it to veterans’ funding that Republicans would find difficult to oppose.

The Bush White House called the combination a political maneuver and demanded a “clean,” stand-alone veterans bill. It argued that the labor-health-education portion exceeded the president’s budget request by roughly $10 billion and threatened a veto unless the measures were separated. Democrats countered that the additional money addressed neglected domestic and veterans’ needs and accused Bush of using fiscal restraint selectively.

Bush ultimately vetoed the combined bill on November 13, and the House narrowly failed to override him. Congress then moved the veterans funding separately, while the broader dispute continued over Democratic efforts to spend more than the administration’s proposed ceiling for fiscal 2008 domestic programs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a breaking-news story from Washington explaining why veterans’ care legislation had not reached President Bush’s desk by Veterans Day and how each party blamed the other.
counterfactuals.output:
**Veterans funding stalled as parties trade blame**

**WASHINGTON, Nov. 11, 2007** — A major increase in veterans’ health-care funding had not reached President George W. Bush’s desk by Veterans Day, with Republicans and Democrats accusing each other of delaying money for troops returning from Iraq and Afghanistan.

The dispute centered on a spending measure financing the Department of Veterans Affairs and military construction. Although both parties supported billions of dollars in additional veterans funding, Democratic leaders combined it with a broader labor, health and education spending bill that exceeded the president’s budget request.

Bush threatened to veto the combined package, arguing that congressional Democrats were overspending. Republican lawmakers said Democrats were using popular veterans programs to force approval of unrelated domestic spending and called for the veterans measure to be sent to the president on its own.

Democrats countered that Republicans had used procedural tactics to slow the legislation and said the Bush administration had repeatedly underestimated the cost of caring for veterans. They argued that the package provided long-overdue money for medical treatment, mental-health services, facilities and the growing backlog of disability claims.

The result was that, despite broad agreement on the veterans provisions, the legislation remained caught in a larger fight over federal spending as the nation marked Veterans Day.

Neither side wanted to be seen as opposing veterans’ care. Republicans said they were prepared to approve a stand-alone bill immediately. Democrats said separating the measure would reward obstruction and weaken their effort to reverse years of inadequate funding.

Until Congress resolved the dispute—or sent Bush a separate veterans bill—the proposed increase could not become law.
